newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Izetbegovic warns U.N. of more trouble on Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Izetbegovic warns U.N. of more trouble on Bosnia.

text.p: Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic warned the United Nations on Wednesday of renewed conflict ahead if major powers did not do more to enforce the terms of last year's Dayton peace agreement.

Izetbegovic, elected as the head of Bosnia's three-member presidency this month, told the U.N. General Assembly his country was a "recovering patient" that would need military and economic support for some time.

He said the Bosnian Serbs must allow refugees to return home and provide for freedom of movement. Indicted war criminals such as former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic had to be arrested and tried and the Croats should dismantle their mini-state in western Bosnia.
"Otherwise, the Dayton agreement will grow from a small and bearable injustice to a huge and intolerable one -- and intolerable injustice leads to new conflict," he said.
The peace agreement, which Bosnia's Moslem-led government accepted only reluctantly under intense U.S. pressure, was being applied only partially and selectively.

"The world, and most of all the members of the contact group, must clearly say ... the Dayton agreement is one whole," Izetbegovic said. "International pressure will be necessary in this direction for a long time."
The five-nation "contact group", which coordinates policy on former Yugoslavia, includes the United States, Russia, France, Britain and Germany.

Izetbegivic, calling for reconciliation and justice, said the country's new government must bring together all the factions in the name of peace and reconciliation. He made no mention of the difficulties in arranging the first meeting of the new three-member presidency, which includes a Bosnian Serb and a Bosnian Croat.

Earlier on Wednesday, the government pursued its campaign to keep up pressure on the Bosnian Serbs and their one-time patron, Serbia. Bosnia's U.N. representative, Mohamed Sacirbey, asked the Security Council to delay lifting sanctions imposed on the rump Yugoslav state, saying it had not yet complied with provisions of the Dayton peace deal.
Sanctions against Serbia and Montenegro, which comprise Yugoslavia, were suspended after the Dayton, Ohio, peace agreement that ended the Bosnian war last year.

Russia wanted them lifted on Tuesday. But the Security Council took no action, chiefly because the United States said it wanted the Sept. 14 elections in Bosnia to be certified formally first by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
Sacirbey wrote that rump Yugoslavia had refused to establish normal diplomatic relations with Bosnia and had not cooperated fully with the war crimes tribunal in The Hague.

There had also been voter manipulation, so the elections could not be considered free and fair, he wrote. "The Security Council should extract the necessary compliance ... before granting further concessions."
